newsitem.title: INDIA: India steel margins seen staying under pressure.
newsitem.headline: India steel margins seen staying under pressure.

text.p: India's steel industry will continue to face difficult times over the next 24 months, analysts said on Wednesday after the Steel Authority of India Ltd (SAIL) declared profits that were below expectations.

"Overcapacity is the name of the game. The supply of steel in India is increasing faster than demand, leading to strong pressure on margins of both government and private sector players," Ridham Desai, an analyst at UBS Securities Ltd said.

Net profit at state-owned SAIL, India's largest steel producer, plummeted to 5.7 billion rupees ($159.2 million) for 1996/97 ending March 31 from 13.19 billion for 1995/96. Sales fell to 147.4 billion rupees in 1996/97 from 151.27 billion rupees the previous year.

SAIL's dismal figures followed a fall in net profit at the private sector Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO), India's second largest steel producer, to 4.69 billion rupees in 1996/97 from 5.66 billion in 1995/96.

"Coal, power and fuel are all more expensive. International steel prices are low, and domestic demand is sluggish. All these will continue to impact the industry," said Shashi Kant, an analyst with Socgen Crosby Securities India Pvt Ltd.
He added that earnings are particularly vulnerable as operating margins in the steel industry are about 18 percent, and net margins are only about seven percent.

Things are not expected to get better as capacity continues to be added, without demand keeping up. According to UBS's Desai, over a million tonnes of capacity will be added in 1997/98 to last year's 18.5 million tonnes.

"Essar Steel will add 900,000 tonnes, while Tisco will add 500,000 tonnes. Next year, Jindal Vijayanagar Steel Ltd will achieve full capacity of 1.25 million tonnes as will Nippon's new plant of 1.5 million tonnes," he said.
Socgen Crosby's Kant said capacity utilisation in the steel industry had been 92 per cent in 1996/97, resulting in production outstripping demand.
"With sluggish demand, heavy steel production led to large inventories. SAIL had 1.3 million tonnes at the end of 1996/97, while Tisco had 242,000 tonnes," he said.

Demand, which at present equals supply, will start to lag by next year. "None of the downstream industries that are bulk consumers of steel have a positive outlook for the next two years," said an analyst at a securities company in Bombay.

He said infrastructure projects were going slow, car makers were scaling back production, and the railways were not expanding. The only steel-intensive sector where good growth was expected was white goods.
While the picture may be dismal for steel companies for the next two years, analysts do predict an upturn towards the second quarter of this year.

"If exports of steel grow, and industrial growth hits nine percent this year, there will be a temporary upswing in the domestic steel market. Demand could grow by as much as six percent if all the factors are right," said UBS's Desai.
Analysts also expect international prices to rise somewhat this year, allowing domestic producers to follow suit.

"Steel prices have not risen last year due to the market conditions. With international prices expected to firm up, Indian manufacturers will have room to increase their prices," said Socgen Crosby's Kant.
